content: Induction of general anesthesia can be a distressing experience for children. Non-pharmacological methods have been explored as alternatives to preoperative sedation to reduce anxiety and improve cooperation during this process. These methods aim to avoid the potential adverse effects associated with sedative medications. Parental Presence The presence of parents during the induction of anesthesia does not appear to significantly reduce anxiety in children. In five trials involving 557 children, no meaningful difference in anxiety levels was observed between children with or without a parent present (SMD 0.03, 95% CI -0.14 to 0.20). Similarly, in three additional trials with 267 children, no clear differences in anxiety were noted, regardless of parental presence. A single trial found no significant difference in child anxiety whether one or both parents were present, although parental anxiety was reduced when both parents were present. However, parental presence was less effective than sedative premedication in reducing children's anxiety in three trials involving 254 children. Passive Child Interventions Video Viewing: When children were allowed to watch a video of their choice during induction, they exhibited significantly lower anxiety levels compared to controls (mYPAS median difference 31.2, 95% CI 27.1 to 33.3) in a trial of 91 children. However, in another trial of 120 children, playing a video fairytale before induction did not significantly improve cooperation. Low Sensory Stimulation: In one trial involving 70 children, those exposed to low sensory stimulation were less anxious and more cooperative during the introduction of the anesthesia mask compared to controls. Music Therapy: A trial of 51 children found no significant effect of music therapy on anxiety levels. Mask Introduction Interventions A single trial of 103 children compared a mask exposure intervention to a control group. While no significant differences in anxiety were observed (RR 0.59, 95% CI 0.31 to 1.11), children in the mask exposure group demonstrated significantly better cooperation (RR 1.27, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.51). Interactive Child Interventions Interactive Computer Packages: In a three-arm trial of 168 children, preparation using interactive computer packages (in addition to parental presence) was more effective in reducing anxiety than verbal preparation. However, no significant differences were found between computer and cartoon preparation, or between cartoon and verbal preparation. Video Games: In a trial of 112 children, those who played video games before induction were significantly less anxious than controls (mYPAS MD -9.80, 95% CI -19.42 to -0.18) and even less anxious than children sedated with midazolam (mYPAS MD -12.20, 95% CI -21.82 to -2.58). Clowns/Clown Doctors: In three trials involving 133 children, the presence of clowns or clown doctors significantly reduced anxiety in the operating/induction room compared to parental presence alone (mYPAS MD -24.41, 95% CI -38.43 to -10.48). However, no significant differences in anxiety were observed when clowns/clown doctors were compared to sedative premedication (mYPAS MD -9.67, 95% CI -21.14 to 1.80; 2 trials, 93 children). Hypnotherapy: In a trial of 50 children, hypnotherapy was compared to sedative premedication, and no significant differences in anxiety were observed at induction (RR 0.59, 95% CI 0.33 to 1.04). Parental Interventions Parental Acupuncture: In a single trial of 67 children, parental acupuncture significantly reduced children's anxiety (mYPAS MD -17, 95% CI -30.51 to -3.49) and improved cooperation (RR 1.59, 95% CI 1.01 to 2.53) compared to sham acupuncture. Parental Video Viewing: Two trials involving 191 parents assessed the effects of parental video viewing but did not report any of the primary outcomes specified in the review. Conclusions The presence of parents during the induction of general anesthesia does not significantly reduce anxiety in children. Some non-pharmacological interventions, such as parental acupuncture, clowns/clown doctors, playing videos of the child’s choice, low sensory stimulation, and handheld video games, show promise but require further investigation in larger, well-designed studies to confirm their effectiveness.
